concepts.bodyMd:
The Vishnukundis (Vishnukundins) hold a primary place among the important royal dynasties of the Andhra-Telangana region, not merely for spreading its name and fame but for introducing new practices in religion, language, and culture. Starting as feudatories in the Krishna-Godavari region, they eventually extended their empire up to the Narmada river and, for a time, ruled the territory between the three seas — the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, and the Indian Ocean. For nearly 210 years, between 358 CE and 569 CE, they ruled primarily over Telangana and northern Andhra lying north of the Krishna river.

They were originally feudatories of the Ikshvakus, and their kings called themselves “Amarpuriswaras” or “Lords of Amarapuram.” Their political stint began on the northern bank of the Krishna river, in the districts of present-day Nalgonda and Mahabubnagar in Telangana. The second king, Madhava Varma, married a Vakataka princess and thereby secured his kingdom. Seventeen Vishnukund kings ruled Andhra Pradesh for about 260 years; the lion springing forward (a pouncing lion) was the royal emblem of the dynasty.

The first few Vishnukund rulers were Buddhists; later rulers adopted the Vedic (Brahmanical) faith. During their time, Sanskrit and spoken Telugu were both in use as administrative/literary languages. In Andhra political history, it is their cultural history — even more than their political history — that stands out as their most glorious legacy. Politically, they established a strong independent kingdom in Andhra for roughly a century and a half; on one side they gained prominence through marriage alliance with the powerful Vakataka emperors, and on the other, through warfare, they subdued the Kalinga chieftains. Their reign also holds a distinct place in the religious history of Andhra.

The Vishnukunds had their capitals at **Amarapuram, Indrapalanagaram, and Dendaluru**.

*   **Amarapuram** is identified with Amrabad, the present-day mandal headquarters in Mahabubnagar district.
*   **Indrapalanagaram**, also called **Sukrapuram**, is located on the outskirts of Tummalagudem village in Valigonda mandal of Nalgonda district.
*   **Dendluru** is located near Pedavegi in West Godavari district.
*   There is also some indication that a place between Bezawada (Vijayawada) in Andhra Pradesh may have served as a Vishnukund capital for some time.
*   Another capital, known as **Puranisangamam**, could be either Sanganigundala in Amrabad mandal or Sangameswaram near Alampuram; the ruins of an erstwhile town lie on the outskirts of Medimankal village near Sanganigundala.

The main sources for the study of Vishnukund history are **inscriptions**. The dynasty's history is known not only from **13 epigraphs issued during their own period**, but also from **8 further inscriptions issued in the later period** — 21 inscriptions in all, of which **16 are copper plate inscriptions and 5 are stone inscriptions**.

**Inscriptions issued during the Vishnukund period:**

| Name of the Inscription | Region |
|---|---|
| Tummalagudem Copper plates (2) | Valigonda Mandal, Nalgonda district |
| Chaitanyapuri stone inscription | Hyderabad, Rangareddy district |
| Keesaragutta stone inscription | Amrabad Mandal, Mahabubnagar district |
| Saleswaram stone inscription | Sattenapalli, Guntur district |
| Velpuru Stone inscription | Tenali, Guntur district |
| Ipur Copper plate inscriptions (2) | Visakhapatnam district |
| Ramatirtham Copper plate inscription | Tuni, East Godavari district |
| Chikkulla Copper plate inscription | Tuni, East Godavari district |
| Tundi Copper plate inscription | Ramachandrapuram, East Godavari district |
| Polamuru Copper plate inscription | Satara district, Maharashtra |
| Khanapur Copper plate inscription | Satara district, Maharashtra |

Besides inscriptions, the **coins** issued by the Vishnukunds, fort walls, cities, and cave temples they built, and objects, tools, and sculptures unearthed in excavations all aid in reconstructing their history. Writings of the period, such as **Janasraya Chhando Vichchitti** and **Sethubandha**, also help in understanding the historical developments of those times.

The decline of the Ikshvakus and the subsequent Pallava expansion paved the way for the rise of Vishnukund independence.

*   Till **355 CE**, the Ikshvakus ruled districts in the middle of Andhra Pradesh, with Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda) as capital, lying on both sides of the Krishna river.
*   The Ikshvakus were defeated by the **Pallavas of Kanchi**, who brought the Krishna river region up to Srisailam under their control.
*   In **358 CE**, the Gupta king **Samudragupta**, ruling from Pataliputra, defeated the Pallavas in his victorious southern expedition and returned north.
*   Taking advantage of this, the **Anandagotrins (Kandara kings)** — earlier feudatories of the Ikshvakus in the Krishna-Guntur region — and the **Salankayanas** in the Vengi region (Eluru) declared independence. In Telangana, the **Vishnukundins** became independent.

From then, the Vishnukunds ruled the Telangana region for some time (first half of the 5th century CE) and the Maharashtra area for nearly 200 years. 

**Vishnukund Rulers (widely accepted chronology):**

| No. | Ruler | Reign |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Indra Varma | 358 – 370 CE |
| 2 | Madhava Varma I | 370 – 398 CE |
| 3 | Govinda Varma | 398 – 440 CE |
| 4 | Madhava Varma II | 440 – 495 CE |
| 5 | Deva Varma | 495 – 496 CE |
| 6 | Madhava Varma III | 496 – 510 CE |
| 7 | Vikramendra Varma I | 510 – 525 CE |
| 8 | Indrabhattaraka Varma II | 525 – 555 CE |
| 9 | Vikramendra Varma II | 555 – 569 CE |

Madhava Varma II is noted to have "taken Vakataka" — i.e. absorbed Vakataka territory — from Prithivishena. **Manchanna Bhattaraka** is also said to have ruled for some time around 570 CE in the Amrabad region.

The first two kings began their political career in south Telangana, in the Mahabubnagar and Nalgonda districts, which made it easier for later kings to expand the territory.

### Govinda Varma (398–440 CE)

*   **Expansion:** Expanded the Vishnukund kingdom on both sides of the Sriparvata (Srisailam–Nagarjunakonda) region through his physical prowess; occupied territory up to the Gundlakamma river by defeating the Pallavas.
*   **Alliance:** Married the daughter of a powerful local chief, Mularaja of Gunapasapuram in coastal Andhra. With his help, Govinda Varma defeated the **Salankayanas of Vengi** and annexed their kingdom.
*   **Northern gains:** Areas on the other side of the Musi river also came under his kingdom.
*   **Evidence:** A stone inscription of his time was found at Chaitanyapuri in Hyderabad; Vishnukund fort and temple remains survive at Keesaragutta on the outskirts of Hyderabad.
*   The **Kesari vagu** (stream) below Keesaragutta gave the surrounding area the name **Gattukesari**, now called Ghatkesar — "Kesari" means lion, the royal Vishnukund emblem. A royal seal bearing this emblem was recently found at Keesaragutta.

### Madhava Varma II (440–495 CE) — the greatest of the Vishnukund kings

**Military career**

*   Fought and won more than **100 battles**; as a mark of victory in each battle, he installed a Sivalinga at Keesaragutta.
*   Built a **Ramalingeswaraswamy temple** at every place he won a battle — these temples at Velpuru (Sattenapalli taluk, Guntur district), Ipur, Indrapalanagaram, and Keesaragutta still receive worship today.
*   With the help of his relative **Prabhakara**, ruler of Gunapasapuram, occupied Kalinga (northern coastal Andhra and south Odisha).
*   In his **33rd regnal year**, attacked the Pallavas again and expanded the kingdom up to the Gundlakamma river.
*   In the west, defeated **Prithvisena**, the last ruler of the main Vakataka line (460–480 CE), and married his daughter — a marriage that secured Vakataka territory for the Vishnukunds.

**Extent of empire:** With these victories, Madhava Varma II's empire extended from the Bay of Bengal in the east to the Arabian Sea in the west, and from the southern ocean (perhaps Pulicat Lake) in the south to the Reva (Narmada river) in the north. Many feudatories submitted to him; one of his inscriptions was found in Maharashtra, and Vishnukund coins have been found across Maharashtra.

**Epithet and capital shift:** He bore the epithet _'**trivara nagara bhavnagata sundari hridaya nandana**'_ ("the one who brought happiness to the beautiful maidens living in the buildings of the city of Trivara"). The identification of Trivaranagaram remains debated — among the possibilities suggested are Tripuri/Tevar near Jabalpur on the Narmada, and a capital in the South Kosala or northern Kalinga region — but it is clear his kingdom extended to the Narmada and Mahanadi rivers in the north.

Because the Vishnukunds and Pallavas were perpetually at war, Madhava Varma II shifted his capital to **Denduluru**, near Vengi, to better guard against Pallava invasions. He also strengthened the walls of **Amarapuri**, his original capital, and appointed his eldest son, **Deva Varma**, as royal representative there.

**Sacrifices:** To announce his victories, Madhava Varma II performed **11 Ashvamedha sacrifices, 16 Rajasuya sacrifices**, and a thousand other sacrifices such as Vajapeya and Purushamedha. It is said he authored a book on metre (Chandas) titled _**Janasraya Chandovichhitti**_, beginning with the title "Janasraya." 

### Vikramendra Varma I (510–525 CE)

*   Succeeded his father Madhava Varma II.
*   Known as _'**Vishnukundi Vakataka Vamsadwayalankara Janma**'_ — one born of both the Vishnukund and Vakataka lines, since his father was Madhava Varma II and his mother Vakatadevi was of the Vakataka family.
*   Held the title **'Mahakavi'** (great poet).
*   Taking advantage of Vikramendra Varma's literary preoccupations, **Madhava Varma III**, son of Deva Varma, declared independence at Amarapura. This Madhava Varma completely exterminated the **Kandara (Anandagotrika) dynasty** and assumed their title, _'Trikuta Malayadhipa'_.
*   Vikramendra Varma — whether driven from the Vakataka throne or arriving from his capital Denduluru — suppressed Madhava Varma III and ruled the Vishnukund kingdom for about **15 years (510–525 CE)**.

### Indra Varma II (525–555 CE)

*   Succeeded Vikramendra Varma I; was attacked by Madhava Varma III with the help of the Chalukyan king **Pulakesi** (the title _'Ranavikrama'_ of Pulakesi found at Yeleswaram supports this). Because of this association, the Chalukyas — like the Vishnukunds — began using titles containing the word _'asraya'_.
*   Defeated Madhava Varma II's other relatives (Palivandlu) and may have merged the Amarapuri kingdom into his own territory, called _'Rajakshetram'_.
*   **Kalinga alliance:** The Kalinga feudatories formed an alliance against Indra Varma II in the northeast; Indra Varma II emerged victorious and saved his kingdom.
*   **Setback:** The Maukhari king **Esana Varma** of North India claimed to have conquered the Salika and Andhra kings, indicating that in his southern campaign Esana Varma defeated Indra Varma II. To restore friendly relations, Indra Varma II gave his daughter **Indrabhattarikadevi** in marriage to **Sarva Varma**, son of Esana Varma, and maintained friendship with them thereafter.

### Vikramendra Bhattaraka Varma (555–569 CE)

*   After Indra Varma II's death, his minor son Vikramendra Bhattaraka Varma was placed on the throne by the council of ministers. His epithet _'**Sakala Bhuvana Rakshabharanaikasraya**'_ suggests the vast extent of his kingdom.
*   In his **11th regnal year**, the Pallava king **Simhavarama** attacked the Vishnukund kingdom; the battle took place around **566 CE** near Dhanyakataka in Guntur district. Vikramendra Varma II won this battle with the help of **Prithivimula**, and as a mark of the victory made donations to the _Vihara_ of Paramabhattarika Devi at Indrapalanagaram.
*   At the same time, **Prithvimaharaja** declared independence at **Pishtapuram**; the districts of Godavari, Khammam, and Nalgonda were then under his kingdom.
*   Vikramendra Varma II later attacked Prithvimaharaja after gathering his army, but **died in this battle**. With his death, the Vishnukund dynasty disappeared within a short span.

### Decline

*   With Vikramendra Varma II's death, **Prithvimula** also became independent and ruled the Godavari district areas.
*   From the decline of the Vishnukund kingdom (**569–590 CE**) for about half a century, up to **617 CE**, **Prithvimaharaja** ruled south-eastern Andhra and **Prithvimularaja** ruled the Guntur-Krishna and Godavari districts.
*   Both were defeated in **617 CE** by **Pulakesi II**, the Badami Chalukya ruler, who thereby extended his kingdom into the Telangana and Andhra areas.

*   Though the Vishnukunds acquired their kingdom through their own prowess and strength, their inscriptions state that they gained the authority to rule by serving at the feet of **Sriparvataswamy**, and they carved the word "Sriparvata" on their coins — reflecting a stated humility and loyalty.
*   They earned fame for proper and popular rule: monks, orphans, beggars, the diseased, and the distressed could earn a living justly under them. They extended protection to Brahmins, giving them lands, villages, and posts, and donated servants, cots, chariots, travel equipment, food, water, buildings, jewellery — and girls — to establish name and fame among the poor.
*   **Extent of rule:** After the Satavahanas, the Vishnukunds are credited as the next dynasty to rule an extensive empire in the Deccan. For nearly 50 years, Maharashtra, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh were under their rule, though Telangana and coastal Andhra north of the Krishna remained under them for a longer period.
*   **Titles:** Because of ruling such a vast empire, they assumed the title **'Maharaja'**; because they protected all types of people they also adopted titles such as _'Sakala Bhuvanaikasraya, Janasraya, Satyasraya, Uttamasraya,_ and _Vikramasraya'_. This set an example for later dynasties — the later Chalukyas wore _'asraya'_ titles, and the Kakatiyas referred to Madhava Varma as their dynastic founder; the kings of Pithapuram and the Velamas made the same claim.
*   **Legal system — 'Divyalu':** Madhava Varma is said to have discovered the legal duties known as _'**Divyalu'**_. When a prince's chariot accidentally killed the son of a tamarind-selling woman, Madhava Varma imposed the death sentence on the prince. Tradition holds that Malliswaraswamy, pleased by this justice, made gold rain at Bezawada and restored life to both the prince and the boy — a story also found in later literary works such as _Nachiketopakhyanam, Prabhodha Chandrodayam,_ and _Panchatantram_.
*   **Territorial divisions:** The kingdom was divided into Provinces (**Rashtra**), Provinces into **Vishayas**, and Vishayas into villages. A Rashtra was governed by a **Rashtrika**. Known Rashtras include Paraki Rashtra, Plekki Rashtra, Karma Rashtra, and Kalinga Rashtra. A **Vishaydhipati** was the governing head of a Vishaya; known Vishayas include Grudhranadi Vishaya and Netrapati (Natavadi) Vishaya.
*   The practice of appointing the king's son as **'Yuvaraja'** for part of the kingdom existed. Some feudatory states remained subordinate to the Vishnukund kingdom, and matrimonial relations were formed with some of them, who in turn helped protect and extend the kingdom.
*   The king was assisted by the **Yuvaraja, Mahamatya, Amatya**, an Intelligence Officer, a Secret Adviser, and other officials.
*   **Forts:** Vishnukunds built several forts, often named for meanings similar to Amarapuram, their first capital — e.g. Indrapalanagarm (Ramannapet taluk, Nalgonda district), Indrakeeladri at Bezwada, and Indur in Nizamabad. To guard their capital from Pallava invasion, they built the **biggest fort in the Andhra-Telangana region** in the Amrabad area, whose wall stretched around **200 kilometres**; construction of this wall was continuous, giving rise to a local saying comparing any long-running house-wall construction to "the construction of Patalabhadruni fort."

*   Villages of the Vishnukund period had a **self-sufficient economy**, with farmers and other occupational groups depending on one another.
*   Besides agraharas, Brahmins were also donated farmers, and servants and maid servants, to cultivate land; Brahmins with knowledge of the seasons developed agriculture with the help of these servants, bringing new lands under cultivation.
*   Inscriptions record that the Vishnukunds dug many wells and tanks for agriculture, through which wet crops were cultivated. Land was measured in terms of **nivartanas**.
*   **Domestic trade:** Vishnukund coins are found at Yeleswaram, Bhuvanagiri, and Sultanabad (Karimnagar district) in Telangana; at Bojjannakonda and Elamanchili (Visakhapatnam district) in Andhra Pradesh; and at Nasik, Khanapur, Nagpur in Maharashtra, and Brahmagiri in Madhya Pradesh — indicating a network of internal trade.
*   **Foreign trade** grew after the occupation of Vengi from the Salankayanas and of the Kalinga kingdom. More Vishnukund coins found in coastal Andhra, ship marks on the coins, and Madhava Varma II's title _'trisamudradhipati'_ ("lord of three seas") all point to the importance of foreign trade.
*   Foreign trade was carried on from eastern coastal ports such as **Motupalli and Kodur** with eastern countries — Burma, Siam, Cambodia, China, Japan, Ceylon, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, Malaya, Arakan — and western countries — Egypt, Rome, Greece.
*   Vadapalli, Bezawada, Amaravati, Motupalli, Ghantasala, Koduru, and Alampuram-Kudalisangamam on the banks of the Krishna mainly carried on international trade, occasionally taking up foreign trade as well.
*   In excavations at **Kudali Sangameswaram near Alampur**, a **gold coin of the Roman Emperor Constantine (306–337 CE)** was discovered along with other coins, showing that the Krishna-Tungabhadra doab was a centre for foreign trade even before the Vishnukund period, continuing through it.
*   The Chinese traveller **Fa-Hien** recorded that shells were also used as currency in the Vishnukund kingdom in the early 5th century CE. Another Chinese traveller, **Huien-Tsang**, wrote of full-size golden Buddha statues at Sriparvata (not found), though copper Buddha statues (4th–5th century CE) measuring one to five inches have been found at Buddham and Amaravati, indicating skilled carpentry/craftsmanship. A cast-iron snuff box shaped like a mango bud, measuring 7 cm, found at Keesaragutta, is further testimony to this craftsmanship.
*   Inscriptions state that sufficient wealth existed for monks, Brahmins, orphans, beggars, the diseased, and the poor to lead a justly-earned life — indicating a strong economy for the period.

*   Vishnukund inscriptions state that "they adhered to the _varnasramadharma_, which is associated with giving gifts and donations." **Govinda Varma** in particular is said to have respected varnasramadharma, and the Vishnukunds tried to ensure that all four varnas — brahmana, kshatriya, vaisya, and sudra — followed their professional duties, though the first two castes seem to have held greater respect.
*   The importance of the brahmana and kshatriya castes is reflected in the title **'parama brahmanya'** borne by some Vishnukund rulers, and in their assumption of "brahma-kshatra" brilliance through performing the **hiranyagarbha** sacrifice. This indicates that the Vishnukunds, who had originally been Sudras, rose in status through performing many sacrifices, and gave many agraharas to Brahmins while also honouring higher-caste members with official posts.
*   **Vaisyas** were engaged in internal and external trade. Among the Sudras, **carpenters, sculptors, and handloom weavers** held a rightful place.
*   **Kanyadanas** (offering girls in marriage) made the families of both bride and groom happy; the Vishnukunds also donated items needed for daily life — sleeping, sitting, drinking, eating — and buildings and jewellery. That Madhava Varma is said to have always served at the feet of his parents suggests that reverence for parents and elders was valued in the society of the time.

The Vishnukunds were followers of the **Vedic religion**, with **Sriparvataswamy** as their family deity; their names reflect Vedic affiliation, and titles such as **'Paramamaheswara'** and **'Parama Brahmanya'** indicate devotion to Siva and to Brahmanical religion.

*   Before the Vishnukunds became independent rulers, the Allahabad inscription issued by Samudragupta used the phrase _'Paramabhattaraka Padanudjyatasya'_, which closely resembles _'Sriparvataswami Padanudhyatasya'_ in the Vishnukund inscriptions.
*   The name **'Paramabhattarikadevi'**, wife of Govinda Varma (the first-generation Vishnukund king), also resembles the name of a Gupta goddess. Tradition connects Sriparvataswamy/Srisaila Mallikarjuna Swamy with **Chandravati (Sandravati)**, said to be the daughter or sister of King Chandragupta. The ruins of the Guptamaheswara temple, said to have been installed by her, stand even now to the north of the Umamaheswara temple and below the Prataparudra fort.
*   It appears that after Madhava Varma II married Vakatakadevi, the Vishnukunds did not patronize religions other than Vedic-Brahmana religion — the Vakatakas being relatives of the Guptas. On the whole, the influence of the Guptas and Vakatakas led the Vishnukunds to become sanskritised followers of Vedic-Brahmana religion.

### Vedic-Puranic Religion

*   Though the Vishnukunds patronized Buddhism (very popular in the 4th–5th centuries CE), it appears they made greater donations to Brahmins, remaining in reality followers of Vedic and Puranic religion. All their names relate to the Vedic and Vaishnava faith.
*   **Indrabhattaraka Varma** and his son **Vikramendra Varma** assumed the title **'Parama Maheswara'**. The Vishnukunds acknowledged that they gained authority to rule through _'Sriparvataswamy Padanudhyanam'_ (worshipping at the feet of Sriparvataswamy), and carved the word "Sriparvata" on their coins.
*   At Sriparvata _padam_ (foot), in Amrabad mandal, is the (Uma)Maheswara temple, which became famous as the northern gateway of Srisaila Devasthanam; **Srisaila Mallikarjuna** also became a popular name during Vishnukund times.
*   In his **33rd regnal year (489 CE)**, Madhava Varma II ordered the installation of a war-drum idol and of **Dantamukhaswamy (Ganapati)**; a Venkaiah (Ganapati) idol outside Amrabad village, along with the Venkaiah _bavi_ (well) and the ruins of a Siva-Parvati temple, and Ganeswara temple in the nearby hills, are connected to this. The war-drum is now kept in the Umamaheswara temple compound.
*   Inscriptions record that **Govinda Varma constructed several 'divyatanas'** (shrines). Vishnukund temples were located in their early capital in Amrabad mandal, in the valleys of the Nallamala forests, under waterfalls, and in caves.
*   The **Anandagotris (Kandara kings)**, contemporaries of the Vishnukunds who ruled areas east of the kingdom, worshipped 'Sambhu' at Vanakeswaram (in Amrabad mandal).
*   **Akkanna-Madanna caves and temples**, though popularly attributed to the historical figures Akkanna and Madanna (17th century CE), were in reality built by **Madhava Varma II** — including the Akkanna-Madanna caves in the Kanaka Durga group of temples on Indrakeeladri at Bezwada, the temples at Keesaragutta, and the Maheswara temple on the outskirts of Hyderabad. Because of similarities in promoting Hinduism, the name of Madhava Varma appears to have been mistakenly attributed to Akkanna-Madanna.
*   Madhava Varma II built many **Ramalingeswara temples**, one for each battle won — at Velpuru (Sattenapalli taluk, Guntur district), Ipur, and Keesaragutta, still worshipped today. To the southeast of the Umamaheswara temple at Amrabad, footprints of Rama are found; to its north is the **Pallaveswara temple**, built by the Pallavas — who attacked the Vishnukunds two or three times — as a mark of their own victory. As the Vishnukunds were Vaishnavas, their Sivalingas are called **Ramalingas**; the same practice of dedicating temples to victories was later followed by the Eastern Chalukya king **Vijayaditya II**, who built 108 Bhimeswara temples to mark his 108 victories.
*   Madhava Varma II was described as _'**Snanapunyodaka pavitrikrita sirshah**'_ ("the one whose head was purified by the sacred waters"), showing the growing importance of pilgrimage and ritual bathing during his time.
*   **Vikramendra Varma** donated Regonta village as _devabhoga_ to the Triyambakanatha temple (God Somagiriswaranatha) in Netrapati vishaya. The Vishnukunds donated villages, lands, old chariots, horses, cows, cots, arts, water, and food along with these grants.
*   Madhava Varma II performed numerous sacrifices and rituals — _Ekadasaswamedha, Avabritha, Avodhauta, Jagatkalmasha, Agnistoma, Bahuswarna, Purushamedha, Vajpeya Shodarajasuya, Prajapatyaneka Paundarika Sata Sahasrayojino_. The practice of donating thousands of servants and girls, and of sacrificing men in the yajnas, reflects prevailing social inequalities of the time. The **avabritha bathing ghat** at Munnanoor fort remains a memory of these sacrifices.

### Buddhism

By the first phase of Vishnukund rule, Buddhism had spread widely in society; early Vishnukund rulers, while themselves Vedic followers, patronized Buddhism to respect majority opinion.

*   **Govinda Varma**, in his 37th regnal year, on the full moon day of Vaisakha month, donated resources for light, sandal flowers, dhwaja water, food, sleep, _arama_, _grasa_, and medicine to the _mahavihara_ built by his queen **Paramabhattarika** at Indrapalanagara, addressed to **Dasabalabali**, well-versed in the 18 branches of Buddhist _Dharma_, for the 14th Arya Sangha at Penkaparra village. He also donated the village of Enmadala to the same sangha.
*   **Vikramendra Varma** donated Irrundero village in 566 CE for the enjoyment of monk sanghas at the same vihara.
*   Govinda Varma's uncle **Prithivimula** built a _mahavihara_ named Tokhalikhata at the capital Gunapasapuram (East Godavari district). His son **Harivarma** built another _mahavihara_ at Gunapasapuram, donating Kattacheruvu village to it, and also built a **Sekya bhikshu vihara** near Tatikonda.
*   Inscriptions indicate that Vishnukund kings likely built or extended Buddhist _arama-viharas_ on all sides of their kingdom. Surviving proof includes the **Govindaraja vihara** at Chaitanyapuri (Hyderabad); Buddhist ruins at Keesaragutta and Kondapuram; _arama_, _stupa_, _viharas_ at **Phanigiri** and Gajulabanda in Nalgonda district; and _stupas, aramas_ at Nelakondapalli in Khammam district.
*   At **Phanigiri**, excavations in 2011 revealed six _aramas_, each with several rooms. Buddhist sites also existed at Jaggayyapeta, Salihundam, Ramatirtham, Thotlakonda, Bojjanakonda, Buddham, and elsewhere in Andhra Pradesh, though most predate the Vishnukunds — the dynasty is credited with major extension activity at these sites during its period. **Saleswara vihara**, in Amrabad mandal, Mahabubnagar district, built originally during Ikshvaku times, shows brick structures and Brahmi-script inscriptions of the Ikshvaku period alongside later Telugu-Kannada script inscriptions.
*   The **Hinayana** sect was present at Chaitanyapuri, Hyderabad, where a Prakrit inscription in six rows records that **Bhadanta Sanghadeva** built a rock house for those offering sandal and clothes to the Govindaraja vihara. This Chaitanyapuri inscription, dated to the beginning of the 5th century CE, is the most ancient inscription found in the Hyderabad region.
*   At **Keesaragutta**, traces of **Mahayana** Buddhism survive, including a metal statue of Mahayana founder **Acharya Nagarjuna**, collected by historian Sri Kurra Jitendrababu; the hood of a snake over the sitting figure's head recalls the iconography also associated with the 23rd Jain Tirthankara, suggesting that Jainism may also have flourished in the Keesaragutta region.
*   The inscription mentions **Pindapatikula**, a special branch of Hinayana Buddhism, and states that there were **18 branches of Buddhism**, with Dasabalabali being learned in all of them. There were several _sanghas_ within these branches; the **14th Arya Sangham** was one. For **Asanapura Arya Sangham**, Vikramendra Varma had the **Trilokesraya Rajamahavihara** constructed, and for its representative Sanghadasa, donated two villages with their gardens. Vikramendra Varma bore Buddhism-related titles of **Mahabodhisatva** and **Paramasaugata**; Sanghadasa belonged to the Kshemacharya branch, associated with Tamraparni (Sri Lanka).
*   The Vishnukunds were the **last Telugu kings to patronize Buddhism**. By the end of the 5th century CE, south of the Krishna river in the Amaravati/Nagarjunakonda region, the **Vajrayana** branch had emerged, into which women, wine, non-veg, and deceitful _mantras_ entered, gradually losing purity — such places (Bomkur, Chinna Bomkur, Pedda Bomkur, Lanjaladugu near Jaggayyapeta) became associated with decline.
*   Another development was growing **Brahmin influence within Buddhist sanghas and arama-viharas**, reflected in the phrase _'Anantha brahmana sambharasya'_ in Govinda Varma's inscription. Brahmins gradually depicted Buddha as the ninth _avatara_ of Vishnu, and some Buddhist centres turned into Vaishnava (Narasimha) centres — Dharmapuri (Karimnagar district), originally Buddhist, came to have temples of Ramalingeswara Swamy and Narasimha Swamy.
*   The last great Buddhist philosophers lived in the Vishnukundin kingdom: **Dingnaga**, a 5th-century logician, debated with **Isvarakrishna** (author of _Sankhya Karika_) at Vengi. Kalidasa's _Meghasandesam_ indicates Dingnaga lived for a time at Ramagiri (Ramagundam) and Munulagutta (near Kotilingala) in Karimnagar district; he authored over a hundred books, the famous _Pramana Samuchchayam_ among them, written in Sanskrit, and taught the Yogachara school — he was the last of the great Buddhist scholars of Telugu country. A stupa and small inscriptions at Basara also indicate his presence there for some time.

### Jainism

*   A Kannada literary work, **Dharamarutam** (1115 CE) by the Jain poet **Nayasena**, explains that the name "Sriparvata" derives from **Sridharamuni**, brother of the Ikshvaku king Priyabala who ruled Vengi country from Pratipalapuram. According to this text, gods worshipping him gathered at a place thereafter called Amaravati; sky-gods showered jasmine flowers on him while he meditated under an _Arjuna_ (Maddi) tree, giving rise to the name **Mallikarjunam**.
*   Corresponding places are found in Amrabad mandal, Mahabubnagar district — Vataverlapalli near **Mallela Tirtham**, identified with Mallikarjunam; the **Pulumavi inscription** (Nasik, first half of 2nd century CE) mentions a place "Siridhan," possibly named after Sridharan.
*   Jain _rushis_ are called "munulu"; the place where Sridhara and other Jain _munis_ meditated may have become "**munuluru**" — now Munnenoor (Munnanoor), also in Amrabad mandal. The text further states that minister **Indraprabhudu** brought Sridhar to Rishinivasa area and made him administrator there for a time as the king of Vengi; since Indra Varma was the first Vishnukund king, he may have been appointed by Sridharudu as administrator of the Amrabad area.
*   **Prithvimula**, father-in-law of the first-generation Vishnukund king Govinda Varma, is recorded making donations to the **Jain vihara at Vardhamanu**, further indicating Jain influence of the period. To the east of Umamaheswaram stood the temple of **Mukmiridani**, and **Mukmirapet** near Munulagutta in Vellatur mandal, Karimnagar district — Mukmiri appears to have been a Jain-related goddess.
*   Jainism disappeared during the Vishnukund period itself. The **Kapalika sect**, which arose during those days — practising magic, mantras, illicit relations with women, drinking, and vulgar dancing — lost popular favour and became responsible for the decline of Jainism; Jain temples were converted into Saiva temples, Srisailam itself being cited by Nayasena as a prime example.
*   It is recorded that **Kumarilabhatta**, an Andhra born at Jayamangala village on the bank of the Mahanadi in Kalinga (Odisha), received Jain education in his youth but later condemned Jainism, attracting many Jains toward Vedic religion. Among those who shifted from Jainism to Vedic religion, **Indra Varma**, the first Vishnukund king, may also have been one.

*   The Vishnukunds established **ghatikasthanas** (centres of learning) and patronized Vedic studies; study of the **Vedas** and reverence for Brahmins are recorded in the inscriptions. Brahmins who studied the Vedas were given agraharas — inscriptions record names such as **Agnisarma** and **Easwarasarma** among the recipients.
*   **Ghatikesari**, the suburb of Hyderabad, is understood to have been the Ghatikasthana of the Vishnukunds, supported by structures of the Vishnukund period unearthed near Keesaragutta. Those who received agraharas were well-versed in education and literature; **Dasabalabali**, the Buddhist guru, is recorded as learned in the four Vedas, adept in all sciences, and versed in all 18 Buddhist _dharmas_.
*   Several kings were themselves scholars, as reflected in their titles:
    *   **Govinda Varma** — _'Shadabhigna'_
    *   **Vikramendra Varma** — _'mahakavi'_ and _'parama sogatasya'_ (as enlightened as Buddha)
    *   **Indrabhattaraka Varma** — _'ghatikavapta punyasancharya'_
    *   **Madhava Varma II** — _'vidyadvijaguru vipravruddh tapasvi janasraya'_These titles show the Vishnukund kings were themselves writers and scholars as well as patrons of poets and scholars.
*   **Sanskrit replaced Prakrit as the state language** during the Vishnukund period. As Buddhism declined, Prakrit — its associated language — also disappeared; notably, the Chaitanyapuri inscription of Govinda Varma, connected to Buddhism, is in Prakrit, while all later inscriptions were issued in Sanskrit.
*   The language of the common people, however, remained **Telugu**. In the Chikkulla inscription of Vikramendra Varma (in Sanskrit), the phrase _'vijaya rajya samvatsarambul'_ appears, in which "ambul" is a Telugu word — showing the influence of Telugu (with "l" used for "lu," and "ambu/bu" for "mu," as an earlier form of "samvatsaralu"). Village names recorded in Vishnukund inscriptions are entirely Telugu.
*   Telugu terms surviving from Vishnukund inscriptions include Kudavada, Velimbali, Marokaki, Kalika, Puranisangama, Peruvatika, Dendulur, Ravareva, Regosam, Penkapara, Irundero, Tundi, Paraki, Vishayam, Netrapati, Vishaya, and _'toluchuvandhu'_ — a pure Telugu word carved on a boulder at Keesaragutta.
*   The Sanskrit poetic work _'Janasrya chhando vichhitti'_ shows references to the Telugu language and is felt to have been authored by **Madhava Varma II**, based on his title _'janasraya'_ — though some scholars attribute it instead to a person named **Ganaswamy**, since the book's actual preface is not available. Its fifth chapter deals with Telugu _Kavitvam_ — _ganas, yatulu, praralu, jati padyalu_, and _dvipada/tripada_ verses. The word _'janasraya'_ also appears in _'kavijanasrayam'_, a Telugu metre work written by **Malliya Rechana** in the early 10th century CE, whose roots lie in this earlier work.

*   Structures of the Vishnukund period demonstrated a new architectural style. Their capital cities, caves, temples, and _arama-viharas_ became key sources for the study of this architecture.
*   In Telangana, Vishnukund forts survive in their capitals of Amaravati (Amrabad), Indrapalanagaram, and Keesaragutta. Below Keesaragutta and adjoining the tank, spacious brick buildings, palaces, Siva temples, and Shakti temples — around 1500 years old — still show their brilliance, containing _garbhagriha, arthamandapam,_ and _mukhamandapam_ like present-day temples. On the walls of **Bhuvanagiri fort**, sculptures of the royal Vishnukund emblem — the pouncing lion — are found, suggesting the fort was originally built by the Vishnukunds.
*   Buddhist _viharas_ and _aramas_ built by Vishnukund kings, royal relatives, and wealthy persons are found mainly at Chaitanyapuri (Hyderabad), Indrapalanagaram, Phanigiri, Tirumalgiri, and Gajualabanda in Nalgonda district, and Nelakondapalli in Khammam district.
*   **Govindaraju** built a Raja _vihara_ at Chaitanyapuri; his queen **Paramabhattaraka Mahadevi** built a _vihara_ at Indrapalanagaram known as the Paramabhattarika Mahadevi vihara — recent excavations near this vihara have identified sculptures of Buddhist _acharyas_ carved on caves at two locations.
*   Excavations at **Phanigiri** revealed sculptures depicting Buddhist Jataka stories, Buddha's footprints, chaityas, stupas, and monks' _aramas-viharas_ and _mantapas_. The Buddhist _stupa_ at **Tirumalagiri**, viewed from above Phanigiri, appears in the seeming distance; the Buddhist _stupa_ at **Nelakondapalli** was so large it was called **Virat stupa**, later corrupted to **Virata Raju Gadde**. Marble sculptures of Buddha and metal statues have been recovered from these excavations.
*   **Chaitya decorations** of the Vishnukund period appear on _mantapa_ pillars found on caves at L. Madugu (near Manthani town, Karimnagar district) and on caves at Gaurigundam waterfall — considered Buddhist _Aramas_. The **Komati caves**, below L. Madugu, are believed to have served as _Aramas_ for contemporary Jains.
*   **Umamaheswaram** (near Amaravati/Amrabad, the birthplace of the Vishnukunds), **Yeleswaram caves**, and **Alampuram** shone as prominent Saiva-Shakti temple sites, reflecting the Vishnukunds' devotion to Siva as indicated by titles like _'parama maheswaras'_ and by the word "Sriparvata" on their coins. At Umamaheswaram, a Sivalinga carved by the Pallavas and a war-drum (_nagara bheri_) arranged by the Vishnukunds survive even today. Among the two cave temples at **Saleswaram**, an inscription in Brahmi script reads _'viswesa kakkalesa'_. Alampuram, in existence from Ikshvaku times, became famous for **Bala Brahmeswara** and the temple of **Jogulamba**; the **Nava Brahma** temples there were built by kings who came after the Vishnukunds. Cave temples of Vishnukund times are also found at **Bhairava Kona**, on the border of Prakasam and Nellore districts.
*   In the surroundings of Vijayawada — another Vishnukund capital area — multi-storeyed Buddhist _arama-viharas_ were carved and built at **Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram**, and **Indrakeeladri** hills. The inscription _'Sri Utpatti Pidugu'_ is found on their walls or beneath their pillars, and similar writings appear at the cave temples of Saleswaram and Pandavulagutta in Warangal district. Some historians believe these writings, made after Saivites drove out Buddhists and Jains, name the society of architects and sculptors; the existence of such a society of architects and sculptors is further evidenced by the Telugu word _'Toluchuvandlu'_ found at Keesaragutta.

The Vishnukunds ruled the entire Telugu country north of the Krishna river for more than two hundred years. During their long rule they introduced Hindu-based culture in place of the earlier composite (Buddhist-influenced) culture, and set an example for the dynasties that followed — their styles of architecture and sculpture were adopted by the Pallavas in the south and the Chalukyas in the west. 

That the most popular later kings, the Kakatiyas, took Madhava Varma II, the Vishnukund king, as their dynastic founder speaks to the splendour of Vishnukund administration. Even as they followed Vedic religion and performed sacrifices and rituals, they also patronized Buddhism and Jainism and made donations freely to their organisations and monks, reflecting a policy of religious toleration. Through their administrative splendour, literary patronage, and establishment of _ghatikas_ at important centres, the Vishnukunds — the first royal dynasty to begin their political career in Telangana — secured eminence for their region and peace and prosperity for their people.

faqs.q: In which period did the Vishnukund dynasty rule?
By which title did the Vishnukund rulers refer to themselves?
faqs.e: The title means "Lords of Amarapuram," their capital.

faqs.q: The Vishnukund capital of Amarapuram is identified with which present-day place?
faqs.e: Amrabad is the present-day mandal headquarters in Mahabubnagar district.

faqs.q: By which other name was the Vishnukund capital Indrapalanagaram also known?
The Vishnukund capital of Dendaluru is located near which place?
faqs.e: Pedavegi is in West Godavari district.

faqs.q: What was the royal emblem of the Vishnukund dynasty?
Who was the family deity of the Vishnukunds?
How many inscriptions in total form the basis for the study of Vishnukund history?
faqs.e: This includes 13 epigraphs issued during the Vishnukund period and 8 issued later.

faqs.q: Of the total inscriptions used to study Vishnukund history, how many are copper plate inscriptions?
Which of the following Vishnukund-period inscriptions was found outside present-day Andhra Pradesh/Telangana, in Maharashtra?
Till which year did the Ikshvakus rule with Vijayapuri as their capital?
Vijayapuri, the capital of the Ikshvakus, is identified with which present-day site?
The Ikshvakus were defeated by which dynasty, which brought the Krishna river region up to Srisailam under their control?
In 358 CE, which Gupta king defeated the Pallavas in his victorious southern expedition, indirectly enabling the rise of the Vishnukunds?

Consider the following statements regarding the rise of the Vishnukundin dynasty:
(I) The Anandagotrins (Kandara kings) were earlier feudatories of the Ikshvakus in the Krishna-Guntur region.
(II) The Salankayanas were feudatories in the Vengi region.
(III) Both declared independence after Samudragupta's defeat of the Pallavas.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
Who was the first ruler of the Vishnukund dynasty as per the chronology accepted by the majority of historians?
Which Vishnukund ruler, who reigned from 440–495 CE, is regarded as the greatest king of the dynasty?
Govinda Varma expanded the Vishnukund kingdom up to which river by defeating the Pallavas?
Govinda Varma married the daughter of Mularaja, a powerful local chief of which place?
faqs.e: With Mularaja's help, Govinda Varma defeated the Salankayanas of Vengi and annexed their kingdom.

faqs.q: The area near Keesaragutta came to be known as "Gattukesari" (now Ghatkesar) because of its location on the banks of which stream?
faqs.e: "Kesari" means lion, the Vishnukund royal emblem; a royal seal bearing this emblem was recently found at Keesaragutta.

faqs.q: In how many battles did Madhava Varma II fight and win, according to Vishnukund inscriptions?
faqs.e: As a mark of victory in each battle, he installed a Sivalinga at Keesaragutta.

faqs.q: Madhava Varma II built a temple dedicated to which deity at every place where he won a battle?
With the help of his relative Prabhakara, ruler of Gunapasapuram, Madhava Varma II occupied which region?
In his 33rd regnal year, Madhava Varma II attacked the Pallavas and expanded his kingdom up to which river?
Madhava Varma II defeated Prithvisena, the last ruler of the main line of which dynasty, and married his daughter?
faqs.e: Prithvisena ruled 460–480 CE; this marriage secured Vakataka territory for the Vishnukunds.

faqs.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the extent of Madhava Varma II's empire:
(I) It extended from the Bay of Bengal in the east to the Arabian Sea in the west.
(II) It extended up to the Reva (Narmada river) in the north.
(III) Vishnukund coins bearing his name have been found across Maharashtra.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
Which epithet of Madhava Varma II refers to bringing happiness to the maidens of the city of Trivara?

options.c: Trivara nagara bhavnagata sundari hridaya nandana

faqs.a: Trivara nagara bhavnagata sundari hridaya nandana
faqs.e: Historians identify Trivaranagaram variously with Tripuri/Tevar near Jabalpur or a capital in northern Kalinga; the exact location remains debated.

faqs.q: To better guard against Pallava invasions, Madhava Varma II shifted his capital to which place, located near Vengi?
faqs.e: He also strengthened the walls of Amarapuri, his original capital, and appointed his eldest son Deva Varma as royal representative there.

faqs.q: How many Ashvamedha sacrifices did Madhava Varma II perform to announce his victories?
faqs.e: He also performed 16 Rajasuya sacrifices and a thousand other sacrifices such as Vajapeya and Purushamedha.

faqs.q: Which dynasty later regarded Madhava Varma II as the founder of their line?
Vikramendra Varma I, successor of Madhava Varma II, held which title reflecting his literary accomplishment?
faqs.e: He was also known as "Vishnukundi Vakataka Vamsadwayalankara Janma," being born to a Vishnukund father and a Vakataka mother.

faqs.q: Taking advantage of Vikramendra Varma I's literary preoccupations, which ruler declared independence at Amarapura and exterminated the Kandara (Anandagotrika) dynasty?
faqs.e: He assumed the Kandara title 'Trikuta Malayadhipa' after bringing their territory under his control.

faqs.q: For about how many years did Vikramendra Varma I rule after suppressing Madhava Varma III?
Indra Varma II was attacked by Madhava Varma III with the help of which Chalukyan king?
faqs.e: The title 'Ranavikrama' of this Pulakesi is found in an inscription at Yeleswaram.

faqs.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Indra Varma II's reign:
(I) He defeated Madhava Varma II's relatives, the Palivandlu.
(II) The Kalinga feudatories formed an alliance against him but he emerged victorious.
(III) The Maukhari king Esana Varma claimed to have defeated him in a southern campaign.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
To restore friendly relations after his setback against the Maukhari king Esana Varma, Indra Varma II gave his daughter Indrabhattarikadevi in marriage to whom?
faqs.e: Sarva Varma was the son of Esana Varma.

faqs.q: Vikramendra Bhattaraka Varma, who succeeded Indra Varma II as a minor, was placed on the throne by whom?
In about 566 CE, near Dhanyakataka in Guntur district, Vikramendra Bhattaraka Varma (Vikramendra Varma II) fought a battle against which Pallava king?
faqs.e: Vikramendra Varma II won this battle with the help of Prithivimula.

faqs.q: In which battle did Vikramendra Varma II die, leading to the disappearance of the Vishnukund dynasty?
faqs.e: Prithvimaharaja had earlier declared independence at Pishtapuram.

faqs.q: Which Badami Chalukya ruler defeated Prithvimaharaja and Prithvimularaja in 617 CE, thereby extending Chalukya control into Telangana and Andhra?
Which title did the Vishnukunds assume because they ruled such a vast empire?

Consider the following statements regarding titles adopted by the Vishnukunds:
(I) They adorned titles such as Sakala Bhuvanaikasraya and Janasraya.
(II) Later Chalukyan kings wore titles ending in 'asraya' following this example.
(III) The Kakatiyas and the kings of Pithapuram referred to Madhava Varma as their dynastic founder.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
Madhava Varma is credited with discovering the legal duties known by which term?
faqs.e: When a prince's chariot accidentally killed the son of a tamarind-selling woman, Madhava Varma imposed the death sentence on the prince after consulting legal luminaries.

faqs.q: In the Vishnukund administrative system, a Rashtra (province) was governed by whom?
Which of the following was the governing head of a Vishaya in the Vishnukund kingdom?
faqs.e: The kingdom was divided into Provinces (Rashtra), Provinces into Vishayas, and Vishayas into villages.

faqs.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the Rashtras (Provinces) mentioned as existing in the Vishnukund kingdom?
faqs.e: The four Rashtras mentioned are Paraki, Plekki, Karma, and Kalinga Rashtra.

faqs.q: In the biggest fort built by the Vishnukunds in the Amrabad area to guard against Pallava invasions, the fort wall stretched approximately how long?

Consider the following pairs of Vishnukund forts and their locations:
(I) Indrapalanagarm – Ramannapet taluk, Nalgonda district
(II) Indrakeeladri – Bezwada
(III) Indur – Nizamabad
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
In the Vishnukund kingdom, land under cultivation was measured in terms of which unit?
Which of the following places is NOT associated with the discovery of Vishnukund coins as evidence of domestic trade?
faqs.e: Vishnukund coins for domestic trade have been found at Yeleswaram, Bhuvanagiri, and Sultanabad in Telangana, besides sites in Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh.

faqs.q: Which title of Madhava Varma II, meaning "lord of three seas," indicates the importance of foreign trade during his reign?

Consider the following statements regarding Vishnukund-period foreign trade:
(I) Trade with eastern countries was carried on from ports such as Motupalli and Kodur.
(II) Trade with western countries included Egypt, Rome, and Greece.
(III) A gold coin of the Roman Emperor Constantine was discovered at Kudali Sangameswaram near Alampur.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
Which Chinese traveller recorded that shells were used as currency in the Vishnukund kingdom during the early 5th century CE?
Which Chinese traveller wrote of full-size golden Buddha statues at Sriparvata, though these were never found?
faqs.e: Copper Buddha statues of the 4th–5th centuries CE measuring one to five inches, however, were found at Buddham and Amaravati.

faqs.q: A cast-iron snuff box, shaped like a mango bud and measuring 7 centimetres, cited as testimony to Vishnukund-period craftsmanship, was found at which site?
According to Vishnukund inscriptions, which principle, associated with giving gifts and donations, did the Vishnukunds adhere to?
Which ruler is specifically recorded as respecting varnasramadharma among the Vishnukunds?
By assuming "brahma-kshatra" brilliance through performing the hiranyagarbha sacrifice, the Vishnukund rulers, originally belonging to which varna, rose to upper-caste status?
faqs.e: This status rise is reflected in the title 'parama brahmanya' borne by some Vishnukund rulers.

faqs.q: Among the Sudras in Vishnukund society, which of the following occupational groups is recorded as holding a rightful place?
faqs.e: Vaisyas were engaged in internal and external trade, while farmers formed the backbone of the country.

faqs.q: Which Gupta-era title, found in the Allahabad inscription issued by Samudragupta, closely resembles the Vishnukund phrase 'Sriparvataswami Padanudhyatasya'?
The name 'Paramabhattarikadevi', wife of Govinda Varma, resembles the name of a goddess associated with which dynasty?
It appears that after Madhava Varma II married Vakatakadevi, the Vishnukunds did not patronize religions other than which faith?
faqs.e: The Vakatakas were relatives of the Guptas, who also followed only Vedic-Brahmana religion; this influence is said to have led to the Vishnukunds' sanskritisation.

faqs.q: Which title, held by Indrabhattaraka Varma and his son Vikramendra Varma, indicates devotion to Siva?
In his 33rd regnal year (489 CE), Madhava Varma II ordered the installation of a war-drum idol along with which other deity's idol?
The Akkanna-Madanna caves and temples, popularly attributed to 17th-century figures, were in reality constructed by which Vishnukund king?
faqs.e: These include the Akkanna-Madanna caves at Indrakeeladri, Bezwada, temples at Keesaragutta, and the Maheswara temple near Hyderabad.

faqs.q: Following the Vishnukund practice of building a temple for each victory, which Eastern Chalukya king built 108 Bhimeswara temples to mark his 108 victories?

Consider the following statements regarding Vishnukund religious practice under Madhava Varma II:
(I) He was described as 'Snanapunyodaka pavitrikrita sirshah', indicating the importance of ritual bathing.
(II) He performed sacrifices such as Ekadasaswamedha, Agnistoma, and Purushamedha.
(III) The avabritha bathing ghat at Munnanoor fort is remembered as a site connected to these sacrifices.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?

In his 37th regnal year, Govinda Varma donated resources to a mahavihara built by his queen Paramabhattarika at Indrapalanagara, addressed to a monk well-versed in 18 branches of Buddhist Dharma. What was that monk's name?
faqs.e: The donation was made for the 14th Arya Sangha at Penkaparra village.

faqs.q: Govinda Varma's uncle Prithivimula built a mahavihara named Tokhalikhata at which capital?
faqs.e: Gunapasapuram is in East Godavari district; Prithivimula's son Harivarma later built another mahavihara there.

faqs.q: At Phanigiri, excavations conducted in 2011 brought to light how many aramas?
The Saleswara vihara in Amrabad mandal was originally built during the time of which earlier dynasty for the use of Buddhist monks?
faqs.e: Brick structures and Brahmi-script inscriptions of Ikshvaku times survive there alongside later Telugu-Kannada script inscriptions.

faqs.q: The Hinayana sect inscription at Chaitanyapuri, recording that Bhadanta Sanghadeva built a rock house for those offering sandal and clothes to the Govindaraja vihara, is dated to the beginning of which century?
faqs.e: This is considered the most ancient inscription found in the Hyderabad region.

faqs.q: At Keesaragutta, a metal statue collected by historian Sri Kurra Jitendrababu provides evidence for the presence of which branch of Buddhism?
faqs.e: The statue depicts Acharya Nagarjuna, the founder of Mahayana Buddhism.

faqs.q: For the Asanapura Arya Sangham, Vikramendra Varma got which structure constructed?
faqs.e: He donated two villages along with their gardens to its representative, Sanghadasa.

faqs.q: Which Buddhist branch, into which women, wine, mutton, and deceitful mantras entered by the end of the 5th century CE, took shape south of the Krishna river in the Amaravati/Nagarjunakonda area?
The Vishnukunds are noted in the record as the last Telugu kings to have patronized which religion?
Which 5th-century Buddhist logician and scholar lived for a time in Vengi and debated with Isvarakrishna, author of 'Sankhya Karika'?
faqs.e: Dingnaga authored over a hundred books, the most famous being 'Pramana Samuchchayam', and taught the Yogachara school.

faqs.q: According to the Kannada literary work 'Dharamarutam' (1115 CE) by the Jain poet Nayasena, the name "Sriparvata" was derived from the name of whom?
faqs.e: Sridharamuni was the brother of the Ikshvaku king Priyabala, who ruled Vengi country from Pratipalapuram.

faqs.q: Prithvimula, father-in-law of the first-generation Vishnukund king Govinda Varma, made donations to a Jain vihara at which place, indicating Jain influence of the period?
Which sect, arising during the Vishnukund period and associated with magic skills, mantras, and vulgar practices, became responsible for the decline of Jainism, according to Nayasena's account?
faqs.e: As a result, Jain temples were converted into Saiva temples, with Srisailam cited as a prime example.

faqs.q: Which language replaced Prakrit as the state language during the Vishnukund period?
faqs.e: As Buddhism declined, Prakrit, its associated language, also disappeared; the Chaitanyapuri inscription of Govinda Varma, connected to Buddhism, remains in Prakrit, while all later inscriptions were in Sanskrit.

faqs.q: Which title did Govinda Varma bear, reflecting his scholarly standing?
In the Chikkulla inscription of Vikramendra Varma, the phrase 'vijaya rajya samvatsarambul' contains which word showing Telugu influence on a Sanskrit inscription?
faqs.e: "Ambul" is a variant of the Telugu term for years ("samvatsaralu"), showing the influence of the common people's language on the inscription's author.

faqs.q: The pure Telugu word 'toluchuvandhu', found carved on a boulder, comes from which site?
The Sanskrit work on poetics 'Janasraya Chhando Vichhitti' is felt to have been authored by which ruler, based on his title 'janasraya'?
faqs.e: Some scholars doubt this authorship and suggest it may have been written by a person named Ganaswamy using the king's title as a preface, since the actual preface of the book is not available.

faqs.q: The Telugu work on metre 'kavijanasrayam', whose roots trace back to 'Janasraya Chando Vichchitti', was written by whom in the early 10th century CE?
On the walls of which fort are sculptures of the Vishnukund royal emblem, the pouncing lion, found, suggesting the fort was originally built by the Vishnukunds?
Which Buddhist stupa, located at Nelakondapalli in Khammam district, was so large that it came to be popularly called "Virata Raju Gadde"?
faqs.e: Marble sculptures of Buddha and metal statues have also been recovered from excavations at this site.

faqs.q: Chaitya decorations of the Vishnukund period, found on mantapa pillars, occur on caves at L. Madugu near which town in Karimnagar district?
faqs.e: Similar decorations are found on caves at Gaurigundam waterfall; both are regarded as Buddhist Aramas.

faqs.q: Umamaheswaram, near Amaravati (Amrabad), the birthplace of the Vishnukunds, later became famous as the temple on the northern entrance to which pilgrimage centre?
Alampuram, in existence from Ikshvaku times, became famous for Bala Brahmeswara and the temple of which goddess?
faqs.e: The Nava Brahma temples at Alampuram were built by kings who came after the Vishnukunds.

faqs.q: Cave temples of Vishnukund times, located on the border of Prakasam and Nellore districts, are found at which site?
